items.title: Metacognitive disengagement and knowledge innovation quality in human–AI collaboration: the mediating role of cognitive offloading and the moderating roles of task complexity and AI literacy
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping the cognitive conditions of knowledge innovation. While human–AI collaboration improves the efficiency of knowledge production, it may also induce creators to outsourcing cognitive work to AI systems. This study conceptualized this tendency as task-level metacognitive disengagement, defined as the immediate reduction of planning, monitoring, and reflection within a specific AI-assisted task, and, drawing on metacognition theory, cognitive offloading theory and self-regulated learning theory, examined its impact on knowledge innovation quality, its psychological mechanism, and boundary conditions through four complementary experiments. Experiment 1 showed that higher AI assistance significantly increased metacognitive disengagement. Experiment 2 revealed that cognitive offloading partially mediated the relationship between AI assistance and metacognitive disengagement. Experiment 3 confirmed the negative effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality, specifically on novelty, usefulness, and developability, with metacognitive disengagement partially mediating this effect. Experiment 4 tested the proposed moderated mediation model and found that task complexity strengthened, whereas individual AI literacy weakened, the negative indirect effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality through metacognitive disengagement. These findings reveal a hidden cognitive cost behind the efficiency gains of human–AI collaboration and provide empirical evidence and theoretical implications for cultivating innovative talent and designing human–AI collaborative mechanisms in the era of artificial intelligence.

items.title: Modeling the Causal Relationship Between Situational Awareness and Some Basic Skills in Futsal Among Students
items.abstract: This study aimed to develop a causal relationship model and identify the direct and indirect effects of situational awareness on some basic futsal skills among fourth-year students at the College of Physical Education and Sports Sciences, Al-Qadisiyah University during the academic year 2025–2026. The research problem stemmed from observing student training sessions, revealing a significant disparity in cognitive abilities and skill-based decision-making despite their similar technical levels. The researcher employed a descriptive methodology using both survey and correlational approaches. The research population consisted of 100 students randomly selected and divided into construction pilot (20 students) and application (60 students) samples. A 14-item situational awareness scale was adapted for the sports context and its validity and reliability were verified (the corrected split-half reliability coefficient was 0.819 and Cronbach's Alpha was 0.866). The Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) and AMOS software (v.24) were used to analyze the data. The results showed that students possessed a high level of situational awareness with a mean score of 33.090 and a standard deviation of 4.856. The study recommended incorporating the causal model into educational and training curricula to link cognitive-psychological factors with technical skill performance in futsal.

items.title: Multi-Aspect Digital Twin for Critical Infrastructures
items.abstract: This chapter highlights the evolution of digital twins from passive data repositories to intelligent systems capable of contextual reasoning, supporting informed decision-making. We introduce the multi-aspect digital twin named MADT4BC, a core DYNABIC component designed to address the observability challenge and increase situational awareness in multi-scale critical infrastructures through AI-based assisting technology. MADT4BC reads and stores heterogeneous data streams from the physical infrastructure, connecting these to a semantically rich digital representation of real infrastructure using knowledge graphs. In response to user requests, AI agents are deployed to operate on top of the knowledge graph: creating, extracting, contextualizing, and reasoning over the collected operational data and the asset information to provide timely responses. We validate MADT4BC through one real-world use case, showcasing both knowledge creation and extraction abilities.

items.title: Owning what one did not make: psychological ownership, agency, and the authorship legitimation deficit in human–AI co-creation
items.abstract: Authorship can align three relations to a work: experiencing it as one’s own, feeling like the agent behind it, and standing answerable for it. Effortful engagement can support this alignment, an arrangement this article calls the labor nexus of authorship, but direction, selection, editing, and authority over release also matter. Generative artificial intelligence can separate initial-production effort from the resulting product without uniformly weakening ownership, agency, or responsibility. This conceptual analysis specifies an authorship legitimation deficit as a mismatch between a particular authorship designation and the experiential or contribution-based grounds expected to support it under prior domain criteria. Separate ownership, agency, and community-warrant profiles distinguish an unsupported sole-creator claim from a supported editorial role, even when the person’s contribution and experience are unchanged. Historical precedents locate the problem within delegated and distributed making. The main contribution is a role-relative conceptual classification. Conditional relational hypotheses concern refusal or qualification of authorship (P4) and later recognition of alternative contributions (P6); agency and observer credit-blame hypotheses (P5a/P5b) concern constituent concepts rather than effects of the deficit. Market dependence suppresses observable disavowal when qualification threatens income; perceived system agency conditions felt answerability while assigned release duties remain fixed. Contribution records may assist later recognition but do not guarantee it. The framework identifies when a role exceeds its grounds while preserving supported AI-assisted authorship and accountability for release.

items.title: PELATIHAN PROMPT ENGINEERING DAN PENGEMBANGAN WEBSITE UNTUK PENGUATAN KAPASITAS DIGITAL SISWA SMK SEMEN GRESIK
items.abstract: Akselerasi perkembangan teknologi Artificial Intelligence (AI) yang masif menuntut peningkatan kapasitas digital siswa kejuruan agar adaptif. Kegiatan pengabdian kepada masyarakat ini bertujuan untuk meningkatkan literasi digital dan keterampilan praktis siswa SMK Semen Gresik dalam mengembangkan website menggunakan AI serta mengevaluasi luaran kodenya secara kritis. Metode pelaksanaan diorganisasikan melalui transfer pengetahuan dan demonstrasi perumusan instruksi (prompt engineering) berbasis kerangka CRAFT (Context, Role, Action, Format, Tone). Program ini diselenggarakan pada 24 April 2026 dengan melibatkan siswa konsentrasi keahlian Rekayasa Perangkat Lunak (RPL). Hasil kegiatan mengindikasikan bahwa pemanfaatan AI mampu mengakselerasi alur perancangan antarmuka dan arsitektur halaman web secara signifikan. Siswa terbukti mampu mentransformasikan kebutuhan spesifikasi pengguna menjadi prompt terstruktur serta melakukan refinasi dan modifikasi mandiri terhadap basis kode yang dihasilkan. Integrasi AI ini terbukti memperkokoh pemahaman logika automasi proses digital tanpa mengeliminasi kendali kognitif dan daya kritis siswa (human-in-the-loop) dalam siklus pengembangan perangkat lunak.

items.title: People offload empathy when they think AI can give it instead
items.abstract: Giving empathy is good, but providing emotional support is hard work. Empathic AI gives cheap and easy support, but may be ethically costly. When AI provides empathy, people may feel less compelled to support others. Four studies provide evidence for “empathy offloading”: when people see AI as capable of empathy, they become less willing to empathize with the suffering of others, even without realizing it. When AI seems more capable of empathy, people—both with correlations (Study 1) and causal experiments (Study 2)—report more empathy offloading. When people learn that someone has received emotional support from large language models (LLMs), they engage less with others’ mental states (Study 3) and offer fewer empathic responses and more social judgment (Study 4). Empathic AI might provide emotional support at any time, but it may weaken our ethical and emotional commitments to fellow human beings. The implications of offloading emotional support may include empathic devaluing and atrophy, moral deskilling, and societal fraying.

items.title: Perceived Craftsmanship Spirit and AI Technology Adoption Behavior Among University Faculty Members: A Moderated Mediation Model
items.abstract: University faculty members’ adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is important to the digital transformation of higher education, yet the motivational mechanisms associated with such behavior remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), and the job demands–resources (JD–R) model, this study used a sample of 374 university faculty members to examine, through a moderated mediation model, the mechanism underlying the relationship between perceived craftsmanship spirit and AI technology adoption behavior. The results showed that perceived craftsmanship spirit significantly and positively predicted AI technology adoption behavior and that work engagement mediated this relationship. Challenge stressors negatively moderated the relationship between perceived craftsmanship spirit and work engagement and weakened the mediating effect of work engagement. These findings reveal the underlying pathway through which perceived craftsmanship spirit promotes AI technology adoption behavior and provide theoretical and practical implications for advancing the digital development and transformation of higher education.

items.title: Perceived Ratings of AI-Generated and Expert-Reviewed vs Clinician-Developed Virtual Cardiology Patient Scenarios Among Medical Students: Randomized Controlled Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Virtual patients (VPs) are widely used in medical education, but creating high-quality cases requires clinical expertise, iterative revision, and alignment with educational objectives. Generative AI may support VP authoring, but direct comparisons between AI-generated and clinician-developed cases delivered within the same educational setting remain limited. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to compare medical students’ learner-perceived ratings of 1 AI-generated, expert-reviewed virtual cardiology patient scenario with those of 1 clinician-developed virtual cardiology patient scenario delivered through the same mobile platform. METHODS A randomized, participant-blinded 2-arm controlled study was conducted in October 2025 during scheduled fifth-year emergency medicine course sessions. Eligible participants were fifth-year medical students who had completed the cardiology course. Students were assigned 1:1 to complete either a clinician-developed VP (CD-VP; n=64) or a ChatGPT-generated VP (GPT-VP; n=67). Both scenarios followed a shared acute coronary syndrome blueprint and were delivered through the same mobile-optimized app (mobile VPs app [MobiViP]) with identical interface structure and branching logic. The GPT-VP was generated using GPT-5 and refined through iterative follow-up prompting under expert review; direct manual rewriting was prohibited. After completion, students completed a mandatory 19-item questionnaire covering realism and validity, cognitive load, self-reported learning and reflection, and engagement and satisfaction. Analyses included reliability testing, 1-sample tests against a neutral midpoint, Mann-Whitney U tests, and Spearman correlations. Full scenario content and development details are provided as multimedia appendices. RESULTS A total of 131 complete questionnaires were analyzed, with no item-level missing data. Mean subscale scores in the CD-VP group were 3.81 (SD 0.64) for realism and validity, 3.67 (SD 0.74) for cognitive load, 3.64 (SD 0.73) for self-reported learning and reflection, and 4.16 (SD 0.64) for engagement and satisfaction; corresponding GPT-VP scores were 4.11 (SD 0.56), 3.03 (SD 0.76), 3.86 (SD 0.77), and 4.28 (SD 0.58), respectively. Compared with the CD-VP, the GPT-VP received higher ratings for realism and validity (Mann-Whitney U=1503.0; P=.003) and lower cognitive load ratings, indicating a lower perceived burden (Mann-Whitney U=1070.5; P<.001). items.title: Provider perspectives on usability, trust, and adoption of digital health tools under India's Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission: A qualitative analysis
items.abstract: Background India's Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) is building a national digital health ecosystem. Uptake by health care providers remains uneven. Paper records often persist alongside digital tools, suggesting a gap between tool design and frontline care. Objectives To explore how health care providers and other stakeholders in two Indian states experience the usability of digital health tools under ABDM, how far they trust these tools, and what shapes their adoption in routine practice. Methods We analysed 42 in-depth interviews with state and district officials, frontline health workers, clinicians and implementation partners in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. Interviews were collected under the provider adoption objective of the parent Digital Health Exemplars: India study. We used template analysis, with Cognitive Load Theory and Human Factors Engineering as a priori lenses. The themes were then mapped to the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). Results We identified six mismatches between tool design and clinical reality. These were (1) rigid interfaces that clash with nonlinear clinical reasoning, (2) separate portals that force repeated data entry, (3) fears of surveillance and unclear data use by AI tools, (4) reliance on paper and WhatsApp as practical workarounds, (5) unreliable networks, devices and power, and (6) one-time, generic training. In some settings, use appeared to depend on incentives and partner support. Conclusion Providers in this study did not avoid digital tools because of low digital literacy alone. They avoided tools that added work without clinical value. Sustained adoption under ABDM is likely to need interoperable, offline-capable tools, clear data-use safeguards and cadre-specific training, addressed in national implementation guidance alongside enrolment targets.

items.title: Psychological pathways to responsible generative AI decision-making among teachers: governance clarity, perceived accountability, decision uncertainty, and AI literacy
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can assist teachers with organizing information, generating alternatives, and drafting feedback. Its use in consequential judgments requires verifiable evidence and professional oversight. This study examines how teachers regulate optional GenAI assistance while preserving professional judgment. Methods Research on felt accountability, metacognitive monitoring, and AI literacy is conceptually integrated to develop a psychological process model of teacher decision episodes. Governance clarity is specified through rule clarity and role clarity, with responsible GenAI decision-making defined as regulated decision conduct. Results The conceptual analysis produces five testable propositions and one configurational expectation. Governance clarity is proposed to support responsible conduct through perceived accountability. Decision uncertainty is modeled as a metacognitive signal whose behavioral value depends on calibration and regulation; AI literacy is specified as a resource for verification, calibrated reliance, and appropriate escalation. Responsible conduct encompasses appropriate delegation, verification, calibrated reliance and accountable human authority, traceability, and escalation or override. These model outputs are theoretical propositions, not empirically established effects. Discussion The framework distinguishes generative assistance from conventional algorithmic advice and identifies task-dependent applications in assessment, feedback, referral, and student support. Future tests should compare unaided and assisted judgment, distinguish process quality from decision accuracy, and examine stakes, reversibility, and contextual dependence. Teachers retain authority to accept, modify, or reject GenAI output, or proceed without GenAI assistance.

items.title: Reference Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The advancement of Generative AI (GenAI) technology has revolutionized the digital marketing sector, yet its impact on consumer psychology requires deeper understanding. Employing a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach based on the Scopus database, this study analyzes the relationships among GenAI usage, customer engagement, and customer trust. Literature mapping reveals that current research focuses on four primary clusters: consumer behavioral dynamics and purchase intentions, visual quality (hyperrealism), transparency and ethical issues, and collaborative creativity efficiency. Based on an analysis of these findings, the study identifies an "Authenticity Paradox," wherein AI-generated hyperrealistic visuals effectively boost purchase intentions but risk triggering the "uncanny valley" effect thereby undermining consumer trust if transparency is lacking. Trust is significantly shaped by the interplay between drivers, such as transparent labeling (watermarking), and inhibitors, such as visual artifacts and privacy concerns. Regarding engagement effectiveness, AI proves superior in stimulating interaction among existing followers, whereas human-generated content remains essential for reaching new audiences due to its empathy and emotional resonance. The study concludes that adopting a hybrid marketing strategy specifically Human-AI Co-Creation represents the optimal approach for synergizing GenAI's technological efficiency with the authenticity of the human touch in the long term.

items.title: Regulating the Future of Surgery: A Comparative Global Review of Approval Pathways, Safety Standards, and Compliance for Robotic Surgical Systems: A Comprehensive Global Policy, Regulatory Framework, and Risk Assessment Review
items.abstract: Robotic Surgical Systems (RSS) have fundamentally transformed modern clinical therapeutics by enabling unprecedented precision, minimally invasive dexterity, and enhanced 3D visualization. However, the convergence of complex mechatronics, autonomous software algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI), and telesurgery presents unprecedented regulatory, ethical, and clinical risk profiles. This comprehensive review provides a rigorous comparative analysis of global approval pathways across four major jurisdictions: the United States (FDA), the European Union (EU MDR), Japan (PMDA), and India (CDSCO). We examine pre-market medical device classification, substantial equivalence standards, clinical evaluation requirements, cyber-security paradigms, post-market surveillance (PMS), and surgeon credentialing compliance. Furthermore, this paper critically addresses emerging regulatory hurdles surrounding generative AI integration, autonomous robotic navigation, liabilities in telesurgical latency, and data privacy frameworks. Recommendations are offered for establishing globally harmonized regulatory standards and adaptive oversight protocols to safe-guard patient safety while fostering technological innovation.

items.title: Repositioning language centres and self-access centres in the age of Artificial Intelligence: From resource provision to human-centred mediation
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has unsettled established assumptions in language education. For University Language Centres (LCs) and Self-Access Language Centres (SALCs), AI systems offering instant feedback, writing support, language models, and conversational practice raise questions about their distinctive institutional roles. This opinion paper argues that LCs and SALCs should not compete with AI as providers of content or feedback. Instead, they should become human-centred mediating institutions that help learners, teachers, and institutions use AI critically, ethically, and pedagogically. After revisiting their established roles in supporting autonomous and self-directed language learning, the paper argues that AI demands a more cautious understanding of autonomy, as apparent independence may conceal overreliance, weak evaluative judgement, and outsourced cognition (Barrett & Pack, 2023; Fan et al., 2025; Zhai et al., 2024). It proposes five future functions of LCs and SALCs: AI literacy development, pedagogical curation, ethical mediation, reflective learner advising, and the integration of formal and informal learning. Drawing on the planned Language Education Institute at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, the paper illustrates how language policy, technology-enhanced pedagogy, and human-centred education may be aligned. Ultimately, the value of LCs and SALCs lies in cultivating judgement, agency, accountability, and community.

items.title: Research on the Construction and Practice of AI Literacy Course
items.abstract: Amid rapid generative AI growth, cultivating AI literacy among non-computer science (non-CS) undergraduates is a key higher education reform priority. Drawing on national policies and domestic course experience, this study constructs a five-dimensional progressive AI literacy framework: fundamental knowledge, risk identification, safety awareness, ethical analysis, governance participation. Pedagogically, the course uses an online smart platform for multimodal delivery, case-based teaching, and integrated process-team assessment. In a teaching practice of AI Safety, Ethics, and Governance with 66 non-CS undergraduates (44 valid surveys), results show a moderate positive correlation between classroom interaction and team project quality; students highly value innovative assessments like team projects and self-designed questions, and most gain achievement from work selected as teaching cases. This study offers an empirically grounded, data-driven course design and evaluation framework, filling the general education gap for non-CS students.

items.title: Resilience and work engagement: the mediating role of job crafting behaviours
items.abstract: Introduction Despite growing recognition that resilience and work engagement are central to employee wellbeing, the mechanisms through which resilience is associated with engaged work behaviour remain underexplored. Grounded in Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined task, cognitive, and relational job crafting as parallel mediating mechanisms in the resilience-work engagement relationship. Methods Cross-sectional data were collected from 332 employees at a large financial services organisation operating across South Africa and Namibia. Resilience, job crafting, and work engagement were assessed using validated measures. A parallel mediation model was tested using PROCESS macro Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap samples. Results Resilience significantly predicted all three crafting behaviours and work engagement. All indirect effects were statistically significant. Cognitive crafting showed the largest estimated indirect effect, followed by relational and task crafting. The model explained 34% of variance in work engagement, with crafting behaviours accounting for approximately 45% of the total effect of resilience on engagement. The direct effect remained significant, indicating partial mediation. Discussion Resilient employees actively reshape their work through behavioural, cognitive, and relational crafting, and this proactive activity meaningfully explains how resilience generates engagement. Cognitive reframing of work as purposeful and meaningful emerged as the most potent pathway. Findings carry practical relevance for resilience training, leadership practice, and organisational job design.

items.title: Reversibility-Aware AI for Supply Chain Decision-Making: A Risk-Adaptive Framework for Human–AI Control
items.abstract: Background: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems move from supply chain decision support towards operational execution, governance must distinguish technical capability from permissible decision authority. This study develops a reversibility-aware framework for allocating human–AI control according to decision risk, recoverability, uncertainty and consequence propagation.Methods: A design science research-inspired approach was used to operationalise four constructs on normalised scales and integrate them into an equally weighted Decision Control Score (DCS), supplemented by governance overrides. Five control modes, from HC-0 (human-controlled) to HC-4 (monitored AI execution), were evaluated using six author-constructed supply chain scenarios. The framework was compared with illustrative fixed HC-3 and risk-only baselines, followed by reversibility and weighting sensitivity analyses.Results: The framework assigned HC-4 to routine inventory replenishment, HC-3 to forecast adjustment and purchase-order quantity modification, HC-2 to logistics rerouting, HC-1 to supplier selection or replacement, and HC-0 to critical supply interruption response. Its recommendations differed from the risk-only baseline in two of six scenarios. When the other constructs were held constant, varying reversibility changed the logistics-rerouting control mode. Across four alternative weighting configurations and six scenarios, 23 of 24 classifications matched the equal-weight results (95.8%).Conclusion: The analytical evaluation illustrates how recovery feasibility can affect rule-based control allocation. Because scenario inputs, weights, thresholds and safeguards were stipulated rather than empirically calibrated, these findings do not establish operational effectiveness or predictive validity. Independent expert assessment and field validation are required before implementation.

items.title: Revisiting Managerial Rationality: Structural Limitations of Agent-Based Artificial Intelligence in Executive Decision-Making
items.abstract: This paper examines the limitations of artificial intelligence–driven managerial rationality in top management, with a focus on agent-based AI models. This study employs a systematic literature review using a PRISMA-inspired approach to analyze agent-based AI models in executive decision-making contexts. Drawing on the contemporary scientific literature, the study conceptualizes AI as a probabilistic decision-support mechanism rather than an autonomous managerial actor. The paper identifies key structural and epistemic constraints of agent-based AI, including probabilistic outputs, bounded rationality, and contextual dependence, emphasizing the need for sustained human participation and oversight in executive decision-making.

items.title: Rigor, commitment, and generative AI: a conceptual framework for student engagement in EAP writing
items.abstract: The increasing integration of GenAI into academic writing has prompted renewed attention to how students engage with writing tasks in English for Academic Purposes (EAP) contexts. While existing research has focused on the capabilities and risks of GenAI, less attention has been given to the instructional conditions that shape how students use these tools. This paper proposes the Rigor–Commitment Alignment Framework (RCAF), a conceptual model that examines the interaction between academic rigor and teacher commitment as two dimensions of the pedagogical environment. Drawing on research in academic literacies, engagement theory, self-determination theory, and visible learning, the framework identifies four instructional configurations (Neglectful, Indulgent, Punitive, and Rigor with Support) and links them to four engagement profiles (deep-agentic, surface, strategic, and disengaged). The framework is further grounded in a triadic reciprocal model in which instructional conditions and student engagement are dynamically interrelated. The analysis suggests that patterns of GenAI use are not primarily determined by the technology itself, but by the interaction between task demands, instructional support, and student engagement. In this context, GenAI may either support higher-order academic literacy practices or facilitate low-effort task completion, depending on the alignment between rigor and commitment. The RCAF provides a conceptual basis for examining these dynamics and offers implications for EAP pedagogy and AI policy.

items.title: Risk Management for Business Continuity
items.abstract: Ensuring business continuity in critical cyber–physical infrastructures requires a holistic risk management approach that anticipates, quantifies, and controls complex cascading effects across interdependent services. This chapter presents the solution approach developed by the DYNABIC project, which pivots around RISKM4BC , a reusable methodology and supporting tools to manage risks that affect business continuity. The approach integrates: (i) a Bow-tie Smart Center that structures threats, barriers, and consequences and is augmented with information from Large Language Models (LLMs) to enrich scenario coverage and generate mitigation recommendations; (ii) predictive business process monitoring that forecasts the performance and risk of incident response workflows; and (iii) a cascading risk model that, based on Bayesian networks, quantifies interdependent risk exposure and updates it in near real time when new evidence arrives. The methodology is operationalized through traceable risk profiles and goal-oriented aggregation that align model outputs with business objectives, as well as through user-facing views that connect live evidence to decisions. A high-level architecture describes how these components interact with monitoring and digital-twin data to maintain a live risk picture for decision making of both human operators and automated responses. A running example from transportation infrastructure (by Ferrovial) illustrates how the methodology produces actionable risk alerts (e.g., congestion likelihood and business impact level), anticipates resolution timelines, and evaluates exposure to external dependencies (e.g., power or communications). We conclude the description of the approach with methodological advantages, lessons learned, and future extensions, including business-goal linking, automated incident reporting, and interactive what-if analysis.

items.title: SECOND LANGUAGE ACQUISITION IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE : A MULTI-PERSPECTIVE STUDY OF PERCEPTIONS
items.abstract: The acquisition of English as a second language (L2) is increasingly shaped by rapidly changing educational, social, technological, and digital environments, particularly in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI). This study investigates the acquisition of English as a second language from the perspectives of students, teachers, and parents, with particular attention to the dynamic interaction of individual, familial, classroom, and technological factors. Guided by Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST), the study conceptualizes English language acquisition as a dynamic and interconnected process that develops through the continuous interaction of multiple contextual and individual variables. A case-study research design was employed, and purposive sampling was used to select participants from Punjab, Pakistan. The study comparatively examines patterns of convergence and divergence across these three stakeholder perspectives to develop a multidimensional understanding of English L2 acquisition in the contemporary AI-mediated learning environment. Its practical implications extend to students, parents, teachers, educational institutions, policymakers, curriculum developers, and teacher-education programmes by informing the development of more responsive and technology-integrated approaches to English language learning. Furthermore, the findings may provide insights for AI and NLP developers, digital learning designers, social-media platforms, and digital content creators to develop linguistically accessible, learner-centred, and context-sensitive English-learning resources. Overall, the study seeks to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of how multiple stakeholders perceive and experience English L2 acquisition in an increasingly AI-driven educational landscape.

items.title: Security Monitoring and Multi-Concerns Resilience Analysis
items.abstract: Critical Infrastructures (CIs) are increasingly complex cyber-physical systems whose interdependencies expose societies to cascading failures triggered by cyber and physical threats. Traditional risk assessment methods and intrusion detection systems are insufficient to address rare, high-impact, and unforeseen attacks, highlighting the need for resilience-oriented approaches that extend beyond prevention. This chapter presents AWARE4BC, a framework developed within the DYNABIC initiative to enhance CI resilience and business continuity through Digital Twin–enabled services. AWARE4BC integrates continuous infrastructure monitoring, advanced attack and anomaly detection, and holistic resilience assessment based on runtime observations. It leverages heterogeneous data sources, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and semantically enriched threat indicators to support real-time situational awareness and evidence-based decision-making. Resilience is quantified through effectiveness and resilience curves capturing degradation, absorption, recovery, and adaptation across multiple concerns, including technical, economic, environmental, and social dimensions. The framework’s practicality is validated through a hackathon-based evaluation using a transportation use case, demonstrating its ability to detect both known and zero-day attacks and assess their cascading impacts. Results confirm the added value of combining security monitoring with resilience assessment. AWARE4BC offers a generic, modular approach applicable across CI domains, contributing to more robust and adaptive protection of essential services.

items.title: Sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers: Implications for biosafety and occupational vaccination – A systematic review with meta-analysis
items.abstract: This systematic review and meta -analysis estimated the prevalence of sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers (HWW) and evaluated hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination coverage and HBV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, LILACS, SciELO, the Virtual Health Library, the CAPES Periodicals Portal, and Google Scholar were searched through 19 May 2026. Twenty-two studies involving approximately 9,000 HWW and 1,722 sharps injuries were included. Random-effects meta -analyses used logit transformation and restricted maximum likelihood estimation. The pooled prevalence of sharps injuries was 34.1% (95% CI, 22.8–47.5%), with substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 98.9%). HBV vaccination coverage was 31.1% (95% CI, 8.2–68.3%) and was not associated with sharps injury prevalence (β = 0.338; p = 0.544). Pooled HBV and HCV prevalence estimates were 2.3% (95% CI, 0.3–15.4%) and 3.36% (95% CI, 1.17–9.23%), respectively. No HCV seroconversion was reported in follow-up studies. Approximately one-third of HWW experienced sharps injuries, highlighting the need to strengthen waste segregation, personal protective equipment use, biosafety training, HBV vaccination, and occupational surveillance to improve worker safety and reduce preventable blood-borne infections.

items.title: Social Risk Management of Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: A Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: With the rapid uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education, academic risks need to be viewed as not only technical issues but as socio-institutional harms that impact equity, trust, and accountability. The methodology used for this study is a conceptual literature review and qualitative synthesis of existing academic research. This study tackles the problem existing in the literature, which is unstructured definitions, by synthesizing the literature to create a complete conceptual framework for Social Risk Management (SRM). The proposed framework places SRM in a unique role, serving as the institutional interface between the introduction of AI and social outcomes, with the role of a mediator and moderator between the raw technical inputs and the negative effects of AI on society. There are four main operational pillars of SRM identified in the synthesis. This study also adds the competency of SRM as a core competency of governance, not only for its ethical dimension but also for being a proactive competency. Moreover, it offers a clear research program for future empirical studies, detailing potential ways to measure SRM and to investigate its differences in various application areas of universities, such as admissions, financial aid, tutoring, and even assessment.

items.title: Standardization, Framing, and Governance Absence: A Systematic Review of Human-AI Relationships Across Engineering, Ethics, and Policy
items.abstract: Abstract AI systems increasingly serve as social partners, companions, and romantic partners, yet governance remains fragmented, reactive, and split between clinical applications and anthropomorphic deception. Current Canadian AI regulation (PIPEDA and the un-proclaimed AIDA) addresses privacy and market access only, while Character.AI and a growing list of anthropomorphic-chatbot suicide cases point directly to the product-liability question that no Canadian instrument answers. This gap illustrates the regulatory break that motivates this paper. In the physcial world, the ethics → policy → engineering loop (EPE loop) works as a mutually protective cycle in which ethics specifies the values a system must serve, engineering builds mechanisms that support them, and policy verifies and enforces them, so that companies and stakeholders share benefits from a standardized technique world. Virtual AI services and products, however, do not inherit that protection. Their values are relational, their mechanisms conversational, and their harms uncodified, so the EPE loop does not close. This systematic review of 169 studies examines where the loop breaks. This systematic review examines how engineering, ethics, and policy shape human-AI relationships between 2022-2026 and identifies challenges and opportunities at their intersections. Following PRISMA 2020, seven databases yielded 395 records; 169 studies met inclusion criteria. Reflexive Thematic Analysis and K-means clustering synthesized our findings. We identify three distinct clusters. The empirical group (n = 30) is characterized by empirical research that documents deception and vulnerability but lacks governance support, producing a regulatory gap. The anthropomorphism group (n = 83) focuses on engagement and safety, and is characterized by the highest standardization gaps that is mostly implicit stated, meaning researchers name the harms but never specify the technique standards against which those harms would be measured. The clinical group (n = 56) shows strong policy engagement but the largest conceptual framing gap, and its high principle-to-practice gap indicates that the gap becomes visible precisely because its principles are codified, yet the cluster lacks broad conceptual exploration of additional missing values such as relational and communicative harms. We show that the three governance failures are three skipped Value-Senstive-Design (VSD) obligations: technical (Cluster 1), conceptual (Cluster 2), and empirical-to-instrument (Cluster 0). We propose a research agenda that closes each gap. For anthropomorphic AI, technique solutions developed into technical standards; for highly regulated domains, broader conceptual maps of the values they have not yet admitted; and, across all three clusters, stakeholder-anchored empirical work under VSD framework. We further argue that VSD values are not exhausted by design values but include ethical values and, potentially, policy values, which is what allows the EPE loop to rotate again. So that the next anthropomorphic-AI suicide case could be decided by a standard rather than by a motion to dismiss.

items.title: Student-LLM Interactions During Math Learning: Limited Epistemic Proactivity Overall, but Within-chat Change Predicts Performance Without AI
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for learning, raising a key question: can learners remain epistemically proactive, retaining responsibility for the cognitive and regulatory activities through which learning is produced while working with AI? Because this responsibility may change as interactions unfold, we examine epistemic proactivity as a developing process. We conceptualize epistemic proactivity through self-regulated learning (SRL) moves, complemented by help-seeking strategies and manifestations of epistemic vigilance. We analyzed these behaviors in 880 substantive turns from 112 secondary-school students completing open-ended mathematical-modeling practice with a general-purpose LLM (Mistral). Overall, students showed limited observable epistemic proactivity: their interactions were strongly request-dominated, with planning, monitoring, and evaluation relatively rare, although low-quality AI responses elicited more explicit evaluation. Temporal analyses qualified this picture: explicit SRL-related moves increased modestly over the chat, but help-seeking strategies became less understanding-oriented. Crucially, these temporal trajectories in help-seeking strategies predicted their post-test performance without AI beyond pre-test and aggregate patterns: students whose requests became more understanding-oriented performed better once AI assistance was removed. Thus, while students had a limited epistemic proactivity overall, its temporal development still was a critical predictor of post-test performance without AI. These results underscore the importance of examining the temporal organization of epistemic proactivity, rather than isolated prompt types, for understanding AI-supported learning. We release our fully-anonymized dataset publicly in an OSF repository.

items.title: The Algorithmic Co-Thinker: A Generative AI Framework for Persona-Aware Computational Mathematics
items.abstract: The integration of Computational Thinking (CT) into mathematics education frequently encounters challenges within Digital Mathematics Learning Environments (DMLEs), which often adopt static, one-size-fits-all approaches that fail to adequately support learner diversity. While prior studies have identified distinct learner personas—such as the Frustrated Perfectionist and the Conceptually Stalled Learner—a critical barrier remains in scaling personalized, real-time pedagogical support. This study proposes a novel framework utilizing Generative AI (GenAI) to transform DMLEs into dynamic “co-thinkers.” Employing a two-phase design-based research methodology, we first empirically validated a four-persona typology through qualitative analysis and quantitative behavioral signatures. Subsequently, we developed and expert-validated a conceptual GenAI scaffolding prototype, comprising structured prompt templates engineered to deliver metacognitive and affective support tailored to individual persona needs. Preliminary expert validation confirms pedagogical soundness and highlights key ethical considerations. The paper presents this integrative framework alongside a detailed discussion of its design principles, operative AI cycle, and embedded ethical safeguards, positioning persona-aware AI as a transformative, yet responsible, pathway for computational mathematics education.

items.title: The DYNABIC Approach and Architecture
items.abstract: This chapter introduces the DYNABIC framework, a comprehensive and adaptive cybersecurity solution designed to enhance the resilience of Critical Infrastructures (CIs) in the face of evolving cyber-physical threats. The framework integrates advanced technologies such as digital twins, artificial intelligence, and cyber threat intelligence to enable real-time threat detection, simulation, and response. At its core, DYNABIC employs a bidirectionally synchronized digital twin to model and simulate cyber-physical systems, supporting dynamic risk mitigation and adaptive response strategies across the four phases of the resilience cycle: Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, and Adapt. The architecture is modular and scalable, fostering collaboration among CIs and Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs). It includes key components such as MADT4BC, SOAR4BC, RISKM4BC, SIM4BC, AWARE4BC, and CTI4BC, which collectively support real-time monitoring, risk assessment, incident simulation, automated response, and threat intelligence sharing. The framework also incorporates a human-in-the-loop interface (AVATAR4BC) to enhance situational awareness and decision-making.

items.title: The Effect of Transformational Leadership and Employee Engagement on Employee Performance in the Service Industry
items.abstract: This study examines the effect of transformational leadership and employee engagement on employee performance within the service industry. As organizations in this sector increasingly compete on service quality, customer satisfaction, and operational efficiency, understanding the human factors that drive employee performance has become a strategic priority for management. Transformational leadership, characterized by idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration, is theorized to enhance employees' motivation, commitment, and willingness to exceed expected job requirements. Similarly, employee engagement, reflecting the degree of vigor, dedication, and absorption employees exhibit toward their work, is considered a critical psychological state that translates leadership influence into tangible performance outcomes. This research employs a quantitative approach using a survey method distributed to employees working in service-based organizations. Data were collected through structured questionnaires measuring transformational leadership, employee engagement, and employee performance, and were analyzed using multiple regression analysis to test the proposed hypotheses. The findings reveal that both transformational leadership and employee engagement have a positive and significant effect on employee performance, whether tested partially or simultaneously. Transformational leadership was found to strengthen employees' sense of purpose and trust in their leaders, which in turn fosters higher engagement and, consequently, improved performance outcomes. items.title: The future workplace: developing the human-machine symbioscape
items.abstract: Purpose This paper develops the concept of the human-machine symbioscape to explain how work environments shape collaboration between humans and AI-enabled machines. Extending servicescape thinking from customer-employee encounters to hybrid human-machine work systems, the paper positions environmental design as a core antecedent of human–machine adaptive collaboration, with particular relevance for service and frontline settings where visibility, coordination, and role clarity are critical. Design/methodology/approach The paper is conceptual and theory building in nature. It synthesises insights from biological symbiosis, servicescape research, sociotechnical and sociomaterial theory, organisational sensemaking and team adaptation research to develop a deductive typology of the human-machine symbioscape as a three-tiered environmental construct, its cue categories, and its design-critical properties. The framework is further illustrated through a structured coding of relevant human-machine collaboration studies. Findings The paper conceptualises the symbioscape as a three-tier environmental architecture comprising physical–digital, socio-relational, and institutional–ecosystem conditions. Across these tiers, six cue categories shape what human and AI-enabled actors can notice, how they coordinate work, and how collaborative routines are reinforced over time. Drawing on Weick's sensemaking theory, the framework links these tiers to enactment, selection, and retention processes, and explains how they influence adaptation speed, adaptation effectiveness, and adaptation persistence in human–AI collaboration. Research limitations/implications The paper is purely conceptual and does not empirically test the proposed relationships. Its evidence base is limited to published studies and illustrative coding, with a strong emphasis on service and frontline contexts. It identifies an agenda for future research around operationalising symbioscape constructs, testing the proposed relationships empirically, and examining how individual tiers and cross-tier configurations jointly affect human–machine work. Practical implications The symbioscape framework provides managers with a structured lens for designing AI-enabled workplaces. It highlights how deliberate choices in physical–digital visibility and interface design, socio-relational workflow sequencing and interaction load, and institutional governance, training, and role architecture can improve the speed, quality and durability of human–machine adaptation. The framework can be used to diagnose service work environments, where frontline employees must coordinate with intelligent systems under conditions of customer presence, temporal pressure, and operational variability. Originality/value The paper introduces the symbioscape as a novel, three-tier environmental construct for human–machine collaboration, extending the servicescape from customer–employee encounters to hybrid human–AI work systems. It adds a missing environmental layer to human-machine collaboration research by systematically integrating dispersed insights on context into a coherent framework that links environmental cue structures to sensemaking and adaptation outcomes. For scholars, it offers an integrative conceptual architecture; for practitioners, it provides a foundation for designing and structuring future workplaces that foster adaptive human–machine collaboration.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Education: Perceptions of Undergraduate Medical Students in Northeastern Nigeria and Recommendations for Trainers
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being adopted in healthcare; however, the perceptions of undergraduate medical students in Nigeria on its role in clinical education remain underexplored. This study examined students’ perceptions of AI in clinical education across four public universities in Northeastern Nigeria. A mixed method cross-sectional survey was conducted between February and May, 2026 using a 27-items questionnaire. Convenience sampling approach was employed, and 200 valid responses were analysed. Likert data and free-text responses were analysed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis, respectively. Overall, 85.5% of the respondents reported a basic understanding of AI, 49.5% reported familiarity with AI in healthcare and 38.5% reported regular exposure to AI tools during their training. Most of the students perceived potential educational benefits: 90% agreed that AI could improve the quality of learning, and 85.5% agreed that it could enhance clinical decision support. However, 86% expressed concern that overreliance on AI could negatively affect clinical reasoning and judgement, while 59.5% believed AI could reduce hands-on practical training, and 57% agreed that it could replace medical roles. Only 20.5% of the respondent agreed to have adequate AI training in their medical curricula, while 72.5% supported incorporating AI into their curriculum. These findings suggest that respondents generally held positive perceptions of AI on clinical education but perceived some concerns about its responsible use and preparation for AI-enabled healthcare.

items.title: The Mitral Valve Heart Team 2.0: Integrating Imaging, Surgery, Transcatheter Therapies and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The management of mitral valve disease is rapidly evolving, driven by advances in multimodality imaging, surgical techniques, transcatheter therapies, and artificial intelligence (AI). In this changing landscape, the traditional Heart Team model should evolve toward a more integrated and dynamic multidisciplinary approach. The “Mitral Valve Heart Team 2.0” may combine detailed anatomical and functional characterization with surgical expertise, transcatheter treatment options, and AI-assisted data integration to support individualized treatment strategies. Advanced imaging increasingly informs not only diagnosis but also procedural planning and patient selection, while AI may improve reproducibility of mitral regurgitation assessment, risk stratification, and phenotypic characterization. However, these technologies should augment rather than replace expert clinical judgment and shared decision-making. This Communication discusses the emerging components of this paradigm and proposes a practical framework in which imaging specialists, surgeons, interventional cardiologists, heart failure specialists, and data-driven tools interact throughout the patient pathway. The objective is not to create a larger Heart Team, but a more integrated one, capable of matching the right patient to the right treatment at the right time.

items.title: The relationship of autonomy with hybrid worker well-being and productivity - the mediating role of managerial culture
items.abstract: Purpose Knowledge work is extensively location-independent, making flexible work designs more common. However, organizations foster various practices regarding the level of autonomy and control, affecting employee well-being and productivity. To support strategic and operative work design, this paper aims to explain the relationship of autonomy with hybrid worker well-being and productivity, considering the mediating role of managerial culture. Design/methodology/approach This paper describes a quantitative survey featuring 1,057 respondents. It tests with a regression analysis a hypothesized model, in which the level of individual work autonomy, mediated by managerial culture, predicts well-being and productivity. Findings The analysis indicated that decision-making autonomy has a direct positive relationship with productivity. Furthermore, autonomy in working practices has a direct positive relationship with both well-being and productivity. Managerial culture mediates the relationship between decision-making autonomy and both outcome variables. Originality/value This paper provides empirical evidence of the relationship of autonomy with hybrid worker well-being and productivity. The academic value of this paper lies in the multiple dimensions of autonomy it addresses, yielding novel data on the outcomes in a comparative manner. As a pragmatic contribution, it provides input to managerial culture design.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Development of Creativity Skills According to Teachers and Students
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has renewed debates on the nature of creativity. This study examines the role of artificial intelligence in the development of creativity skills among middle school teachers and students through comparative perspectives. Using a qualitative case study design, the research involved 87 participants—42 teachers from different subject areas and 45 eighth-grade students—from public middle schools in Bursa, Turkey, during the 2025–2026 academic year. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed via content analysis. The findings reveal that AI plays a dual role in the creative process: it facilitates idea generation and imagination, yet may restrict originality when used without pedagogical guidance. While students tend to view artificial intelligence as a tool that accelerates production, teachers emphasize risks such as cognitive offloading and superficial learning. Artificial intelligence becomes an effective educational tool only when embedded within ethically grounded, teacher-guided, and AI literacy–oriented frameworks. Subject-based analyses show that, particularly in Science and Mathematics, teachers position AI as a supportive cognitive partner that facilitates visualization and conceptual understanding, yet caution that unguided use may replace deep learning with surface-level content production.

items.title: The Study of Digital Transformation, Artificial Intelligence and Their Implications for Future Research
items.abstract: Digital transformation changes the conditions under which organizations produce and use knowledge. Artificial intelligence adds new ways to search, predict, generate, and evaluate information. Yet greater use of these tools does not establish that research becomes more reliable or more original. This paper develops a critical narrative review and descriptive secondary-data analysis to examine that distinction. Selected publications on organizational change, AI-assisted work, scientific discovery, and governance provide the conceptual foundation. Published statistics from Stanford's AI Index and Eurostat illustrate changes in adoption between 2023 and 2025. The two series are analysed separately because their populations and measurement procedures differ. The evidence indicates expanding use, but adoption statistics cannot demonstrate causal improvements in research quality. An original conceptual framework links digital foundations and AI capabilities with changes in research practice, conditioned by human expertise, institutional arrangements, and governance. Four propositions translate the framework into questions for future testing. The proposed agenda prioritizes reproducibility, task-specific evaluation, skill development, equitable participation, and preservation of intellectual diversity. The paper concludes that future research should evaluate the complete knowledge-production process, including verification and correction costs, rather than treating faster output as sufficient evidence of progress. No primary survey, experiment, or model validation is claimed. The contribution is an integrated account of how organizations can study AI-enabled transformation while maintaining the evidentiary standards needed for credible knowledge

items.title: The Usability of Ranked Choice Voting in Digital Ballot Formats
items.abstract: ObjectiveThree digital ranked choice voting ballots were investigated to assess the impact of formatting on usability.BackgroundRanked choice voting (RCV) is a ballot format that allows voters to rank candidate choices in order of preference. The design of the ballot has a notable impact on usability, and this remains a challenge for RCV.MethodThis experiment investigated the usability of three RCV electronic ballot formats (bubble grid, column, and hand-numbered). Completion times, errors, subjective usability ratings, and trust data were collected.ResultsThe three formats took subjects 50-70 seconds on average to vote for a single contest. The ballots also had high error rates, which ranged from 23-38%. The hand-numbered format had the worst performance, as it had the highest completion times, error rates, and the lowest subjective usability ratings.ConclusionThis research highlights usability issues with RCV digital ballots. The formats tested were inefficient and ineffective, and performed poorly in comparison to previously tested plurality digital ballots.ApplicationThis experiment raises concerns about the scalability of RCV to larger elections. Ballots with RCV take longer to vote on and have higher error rates, which should be taken into consideration by election administrators.

items.title: Understanding Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Audit in Nigeria: Will AI Replace the Auditor? A Qualitative Phenomenological Inquiry
items.abstract: This study qualitatively inquired into artificial intelligence and the future of audit in Nigeria, specifically investigating whether AI will replace the human auditor. A qualitative phenomenological design was adopted. Twenty-eight (28) participants were purposively selected across Lagos, Abuja, and Port Harcourt, comprising Big 4 and mid-tier audit partners, audit managers/seniors with 10+ years of experience, ICAN/ANAN/FRCN regulators, and audited clients including CFOs and Audit Committee chairs. Data were collected via semi-structured indepth interviews between January and May 2025. Data saturation was achieved at the 23rd interview. Thematic analysis was performed using the Braun and Clarke (2006) framework assisted by NVivo. Results reveal that AI is augmenting, not replacing, human auditors. Four distinct AI implementation levels emerged: Assisted Audit (e.g., IDEA, Excel), Augmented Audit (e.g., Power BI, ACL), Autonomous Testing (e.g., RPA, Machine Learning anomaly detection), and Advisory Assurance (e.g., Generative AI for reporting). AI deployment improved audit efficiency by 60% and increased anomaly detection from 35% to 82%. Key barriers to adoption include technophobia (78%), unstructured client data (72%), tool costs (65%), and a regulatory vacuum regarding AI audit evidence under ISA 500 (60%). The study proposes a Human-AI Collaboration Model (70-30 Model), where AI performs 70% of routine data tasks, and human auditors provide 30% high-level professional judgement, ethics, and skepticism. This represents the first phenomenological study in Nigeria exploring the lived experiences of senior practitioners on the AI replacement debate.

items.title: University students’ overreliance on generative AI feedback in the learning process: the effects of perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and metacognitive monitoring
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has introduced an important question in education, when AI provides immediate and reliable feedback, do students use it as a learning support tool or gradually rely on it as a substitute for their own cognitive efforts? Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, Cognitive Offloading Theory, and Metacognitive Monitoring Theory, this study develops a theoretical model to explain the formation process of undergraduate students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Specifically, this study examines the relationships among perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and overreliance on GAI feedback, while further exploring how metacognitive monitoring levels shape this process. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 600 undergraduate students, and structural equation modeling was performed using AMOS 31.0. The results showed that perceived cognitive load significantly and positively predicted cognitive offloading, which further contributed to students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Meanwhile, perceived cognitive load also directly predicted overreliance on GAI feedback. Bootstrap analysis further confirmed that cognitive offloading mediated the relationship between perceived cognitive load and overreliance on GAI feedback. In addition, this study established separate structural equation models for students with different levels of metacognitive monitoring and found distinct patterns in the formation of GAI feedback overreliance. Specifically, students with lower metacognitive monitoring were more likely to be influenced by cognitive pressure during learning, showing a more prominent direct relationship between perceived cognitive load and GAI feedback overreliance. This finding suggests that these students tend to rely more directly on GAI feedback when facing higher cognitive demands. In contrast, students with higher metacognitive monitoring demonstrated a more evident cognitive regulation process, in which cognitive offloading played a more important role in linking perceived cognitive load with GAI feedback overreliance. This indicates that these students may actively adjust their cognitive resource allocation when using GAI, although continuous cognitive offloading may still increase their dependence on AI-generated feedback.

items.title: Unpacking Ethical, Privacy, And Governance Risks in AI-IoT Based Healthcare Environments: A thematic analysis
items.abstract: Objective: The paper aimed to examine ethical, privacy, and governance challenges in AI-IoT (Artificial Intelligence-based Internet of Things) healthcare environments. Design: A total of 39 peer-reviewed open-access studies were screened and used for a systematic review using the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework. A multi-stage thematic analysis was used for identifying recurring patterns within the literature and answering the research questions. Results/outcomes: The identified challenges in the AI-IoT healthcare ecosystems, arising from the thematic analysis, are privacy and continuous surveillance, algorithmic bias and lack of explainability, limitations for informed consent, and fragmented governance and accountability. Conclusion: The findings, in sync with STS theory, indicate that challenges in AI-IoT healthcare systems cannot be addressed solely through technological innovations. In response, the study proposed an Integrated Human-Centric Trust Framework to integrate human intervention with technological advancements.

items.title: Use of Artificial Intelligence among Undergraduate Medical Students at Dhaka National Medical College: A Descriptive Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Background: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly increasing among university students worldwide. However, little is known about how undergraduate medical students in Bangladesh engage with AI tools in their education. Objective: To assess the pattern of using AI and the self-reported knowledge and attitude regarding AI among undergraduate medical students of Dhaka National Medical College (DNMC). Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 5th-year MBBS students of DNMC from December 2025 to July 2026 (4th-year students were excluded). By convenience type of non-probability sampling, 125 medical students completed a structured, self-administered questionnaire distributed as a Google Form through students' WhatsApp number. The questionnaire included sociodemographic data, patterns of AI use, and a 10-item, 5-point Likert scale for assessment of self-reported knowledge and attitudes (range 10 to 50). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, the chi-square test, independent t-test, and ANOVA; p<0.05 was considered significant. Results: Mean age of 125 students was 21.7±1.7 years, among them 56.0% were female. Almost all respondents (97.6%) were familiar with AI. Most of them (89.6%) were current users, most commonly of ChatGPT (81.2%) and Gemini (32.1%). Majority of them (81.3%) thought that AI would be beneficial to their future career and 74.2% felt it should be taught to all medical students, 41.1% felt confident about replacement of medical specialities. Half of respondents (50.0%) were concerned about AI-generated misinformation, and 79.3% reported at least occasional difficulty verifying AI-generated academic content. The composite knowledge–attitude score (mean 37.2±6.0 of 50) rose significantly with academic year (p=0.023, driven by a 1st- versus 5th-year difference). Gender and current AI-use status were not significantly associated with the score. Conclusion: Most of the undergraduate medical students of DNMC have familiarity with use AIs and positive attitudes of it use for their learning. However, some of them are concerned about the misinformation may be produced by the AIs. Hence, structured AI-literacy training, from the first year of the MBBS curriculum, is a demand of the time. Many students now turn to smartphone artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots late at night for private emotional comfort. This study assessed the prevalence of AI chatbot usage for emotional support, user perception, and emotional reliance among healthcare trainees in rural South India.

items.title: Using Generative AI for Behavioural Research Effectively and Responsibly: a BR-UK Statement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across the behavioural research lifecycle. It may improve the efficiency and quality of research, but rapid, uncritical adoption carries risks to research integrity: algorithmic bias, ethical concerns around consent, privacy and plagiarism, erosion of researchers’ skills and public trust, and environmental costs. This Open Letter presents Behavioural Research UK’s (BR-UK) statement on using generative AI effectively and responsibly in behavioural research. It was informed by existing guidance and expert consultation. The statement sets out BR-UK’s four key propositions: (1) research ethics and integrity principles must include AI concerns; (2) AI should assist, but not replace, researchers through a human-in-the-loop approach; (3) rigorous evaluation of AI use is essential; and (4) coordinated stakeholder action is needed to move from identifying risks to practical solutions. It then provides recommendations and points to practical tools, such as decision aids and checklists for declaring AI use, for seven stakeholder groups, namely research-generating institutions, funders, publication outlets, behavioural research networks and communities, AI platform and tool providers, individual researchers, and research users. The statement will be reviewed annually until 2028, the duration of BR-UK, as technology and evidence evolve.

items.title: Versioned Governance for Frontier AI: A Software-Engineering-Inspired Approach
items.abstract: Abstract Background FrontierAI laboratories govern deployed systems via model specifications, usage policies, and safety frameworks. These governance documents undergo repeated revisions, yet current practices rarely distinguish substantive normative policy changes from mere editorial clarifications. This produces silent drift: continuous normative modification without clear documentation of changes, reasons for modification, and the institutional authority under which changes were made. The following are examples of an AI API that identifies new drugs and vaccines for a given disease, scaling from a simple “Name that drug!” function to much more advanced models. This paper reviews the revision histories for five publicly available AI governance instruments that are slated for release between 2019 and 2025; OpenAI usage policies and Model Specific, Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. This paper identifies the areas where current practices seemed aligned with formal versioning discipline, and it pinpointed the areas where there are persistent implementation gaps. Version number tracking vocabulary is becoming more frequent at the whole document level, while the specific term level is still not being used. The type of AI disruptive technology that incites a substantial shift from a normative route is an exogenous shock. Current changelogs are descriptive, but they are not change classified. Explicit structural rollback mechanisms are not found in any of the examined instruments. Through this analysis, we realize that there are genuine limits of the software-as-a-policy analogy, taking these limitations as hard design constraints for possible AI regulation instead of unconsidered counter-arguments. Implications: AI labs can “self-engineer” a lightweight globally adaptable, versioning approach to formally defined meta-changes, clause granular history logs, design rollback aware implementations, and misclassification preserved as independently audit-bounded events that can be independently audited by regulators/independent auditors and formally accepted by regulators as an independent practice. Does not imply specific compelling AI system substantive policy content.

items.title: Von menschzentrierter KI zu nachhaltigen autonomen Systemen: eine soziotechnische Forschungs- und Entwicklungsagenda
items.abstract: Der Beitrag entwickelt aus den Erfahrungen des Projekts Künstlich Menschlich Intelligent eine soziotechnische Forschungs- und Entwicklungsagenda für die nächste Phase der digitalen und nachhaltigen Transformation (Twin Transformation). Im Zentrum steht die Frage, unter welchen Bedingungen datenbasierte Technologien und insbesondere KI-Agenten und autonome Systeme zu humangerechter Arbeit, Effizienz, organisationaler Wertschöpfung und Nachhaltigkeit beitragen können. Ausgehend von einem Dreiklang aus Wirkung, Gestaltung und Befähigung wird gezeigt, dass die nächste Welle der digitalen Transformation nicht als lineare technische Implementierung verstanden werden kann, sondern als reflexiver Gestaltungsprozess, in dem Mensch, Technik und Organisation gemeinsam unter dem Leitbild der Nachhaltigkeit weiterentwickelt werden. Die Projekterfahrungen und aktuelle Erkenntnisse machen zentrale Ambivalenzen sichtbar: Digitalisierung bedeutet nicht automatisch KI-Readiness; niedrigschwellige KI-Nutzung ersetzt keine organisationale Gestaltungsfähigkeit; und Entlastung durch KI kann zugleich Arbeitsverdichtung, Verantwortungsverschiebung oder De-Skilling erzeugen. Darauf aufbauend formuliert der Beitrag zukünftige Forschungsfelder zu mehrdimensionaler Wirkungsmessung, Mensch-KI-Interaktion, Human-AI Teaming, Ko-Adaption, Partizipation, KI-Governance, Verantwortlichkeit, Aufsicht, Kompetenzentwicklung, Transfer, digitaler Souveränität, Abhängigkeiten und Lock-in-Effekten. Besondere Aufmerksamkeit gilt kleinen und mittleren Unternehmen sowie ressourcenbeschränkten Organisationen, die für nachhaltige KI-Nutzung Orientierungswissen, Methoden, Demonstratoren und intermediäre Transferstrukturen benötigen.

items.title: When Assistance Becomes Infrastructure
items.abstract: Debates about the future of artificial intelligence often focus on a single decisive moment, when machines surpass humans. This essay examines a less visible path: AI may become infrastructure through a series of local, reasonable decisions that no one makes as a whole. We follow one question across three stages: can we still go back? First, services are redesigned around AI and non-AI channels close, a form of coercion without a coercer. Second, the human role shifts from producing to ratifying, and the skills needed to check AI output erode, as early clinical and labor-market evidence suggests. Third, the ability to compare work with and without AI disappears, so that a society may lose not only a capability but also the knowledge that it existed. A simple model shows how two reinforcing loops create hysteresis, in which the way back costs more than the way in. We then discuss brakes (laws, fallback options, reserves of skill), structural forcings (public debt, the decline of public research, geopolitical rivalry), and four possible end states: integration, bypass, managed coexistence, and partial return. We argue that the key question is whether human alternatives remain reproducible and measurable.

items.title: When Does GenAI Use Support Critical Thinking? A Cross-Cultural Structural Account of Transactive Memory with GenAI
items.abstract: Whether generative AI (GenAI) use helps or hinders critical thinking remains contested, and existing accounts emphasize exposure to the tool rather than how a person structures their engagement with it. Extending Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) theory to human-AI partnerships, we test a structural account of critical thinking in GenAI-assisted academic work among 891 college students in the United States and Türkiye. Self-appraised thinking ability and confidence in the partnership shaped how much practical experience a person built up with GenAI, but neither predicted critical thinking directly. That experience mattered only through two downstream behaviors, dividing and coordinating cognitive labor with the tool, and actively reworking its output rather than accepting it as given. A multigroup comparison found this structure largely invariant, with two theoretically interpretable exceptions. This study offers a structural, TMS-based account of critical thinking in GenAI-assisted work.

items.title: When Employees Perceive AI as a Partner: How Human–Machine Relationship Perception Shapes Employee Innovative Behavior
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into organizational work, highlighting the importance of employees’ relational perceptions of AI for innovative behavior. Drawing on cognitive appraisal and social exchange theories, this study examines how human–machine relationship perception (HMRP) influences employee innovative behavior through psychological empowerment, with perceived organizational support as a moderator. Three-wave, multi-source data were collected from 428 employee–supervisor dyads across 27 technology-intensive firms. Results indicate that HMRP positively predicts innovative behavior (β = 0.360, p < 0.001) and psychological empowerment (β = 0.470, p < 0.001). Psychological empowerment positively predicts innovative behavior (β = 0.320, p < 0.001) and mediates the HMRP–innovation relationship (indirect effect = 0.150, 95% CI [0.108, 0.198]), explaining 41.7% of the total effect. Perceived organizational support strengthens the HMRP–empowerment relationship (β = 0.130, p = 0.001), with conditional indirect effects increasing from 0.109 to 0.192 and a moderated mediation index of 0.042 (95% CI [0.018, 0.071]). These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by identifying relational cognition and psychological empowerment as mechanisms linking AI collaboration to employee innovation and highlighting the importance of organizational support.
